name: Numbers
author: Jewish and Christian tradition names Moses as the author of Numbers and the other four books of the Law. Moses was an Israelite raised in the Egyptian royal court who became the prophet and leader who brought Israel out of slavery in Egypt and through the desert. Many scholars instead see the book as gathered from older records, laws and stories over several centuries, reaching its final form around the time of the exile in Babylon or soon after (500s–400s BC).
audience: Traditionally, the first hearers were the new generation of Israelites camped on the plains of Moab, east of the Jordan River, about to enter the land of Canaan after their parents' generation had died in the desert. Many scholars also see the finished book as speaking to later Israelites, possibly exiles in Babylon or those returning home, who were themselves waiting to settle again in the promised land.
era: The book covers roughly forty years of Israel's life as a wandering people in the desert, from Mount Sinai to the edge of Canaan. The date of the exodus from Egypt is debated, with the two main views placing it in the 1400s BC or the 1200s BC. Canaan was then a patchwork of small walled city-states, often under Egyptian influence, surrounded by neighbouring peoples such as the Edomites, Moabites, Amorites and Midianites. Israel lived in tents, organised by tribes and clans, with the portable worship tent called the tabernacle at the centre of the camp.

notes.6:22: Two tiny silver scrolls found in a tomb near Jerusalem, dated around 600 BC, carry a version of this blessing, the oldest surviving copy of any words found in the Bible.
notes.12:1: Cush was a land south of Egypt, roughly modern Sudan; some readers think the wife meant here is Zipporah, others a second wife.
notes.20:1: Most readers understand the story here as jumping forward about thirty-eight years, from the second year after leaving Egypt to near the fortieth.
notes.20:14: Edom lay south-east of the Dead Sea; its people were seen as descendants of Esau, Jacob's brother, and the King's Highway was a major trade route through it.
notes.20:22: Later in Numbers, Aaron's death on Mount Hor is dated to the fifth month of the fortieth year after leaving Egypt.
notes.21:4: Centuries later, around 700 BC, King Hezekiah destroyed a bronze snake kept in Jerusalem, said to be the one Moses made; it was called Nehushtan, and people had been offering incense to it.
notes.21:10: This passage quotes the Book of the Wars of the Lord, an ancient collection of songs or poems that has since been lost.
notes.21:33: Bashan was a fertile highland east of the Sea of Galilee, famous in ancient times for its rich pastures, strong cattle and oak trees.
notes.22:1: An inscription found at Deir Alla in Jordan, dated around 800 BC, mentions a seer named Balaam son of Beor, showing he was remembered beyond Israel.
notes.25:1: Baal was the chief storm and fertility god worshipped by Canaanites and neighbours; Baal of Peor was the local form honoured on a mountain called Peor in Moab.
notes.28:26: The Festival of Weeks came seven weeks after Passover at the wheat harvest; Greek-speaking Jews later called it Pentecost, meaning fiftieth.
notes.29:1: This first-day-of-the-seventh-month gathering, marked by trumpet blasts, became the Jewish New Year, Rosh Hashanah, in later times.
notes.29:7: The tenth day of the seventh month is the Day of Atonement, Yom Kippur, Israel's most solemn day of fasting and cleansing.
notes.29:12: This week-long feast is the Festival of Shelters, or Tabernacles, an autumn harvest celebration when Israelites lived in temporary huts for the week.
notes.31:1: The Midianites were a desert people living around the edges of Israel's route; Moses' own wife Zipporah and father-in-law Jethro were Midianites.
notes.32:1: Gilead and Jazer were rich grazing lands east of the Jordan River, in what is now Jordan, outside the land of Canaan proper.
notes.33:1: This list of camping places traces the whole desert journey; many of the sites named can no longer be identified with certainty today.
notes.35:9: The book of Joshua later names the six cities of refuge, three on each side of the Jordan River.
